summary: Surveys proposals made during an effort to address scalability, multihoming and inter-domain traffic engineering problems in Internet routing and addressing. It recommends directions the IETF might take. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The internet's address book is growing too large to handle. This note compares ideas for organizing it better and suggests which to pursue.

subtitle: A survey of proposed solutions to Internet routing scalability problems.

tldr.problem: The Internet's routing and addressing system faces three interconnected challenges: the global routing table is growing too large to scale, multihoming (connecting to multiple service providers) creates inefficiencies, and inter-domain traffic engineering lacks adequate mechanisms for control.
tldr.mechanism: The Routing Research Group reviewed over a dozen proposals for architectural changes, including approaches that separate network identity from location (LISP, RANGI, ILNP), hierarchical aggregation schemes (hIPv4), mapping-based systems, and evolutionary approaches. For each proposal, the document captures the key ideas, benefits, costs, and technical critiques.
tldr.outcome: Although the RRG did not reach consensus on a single solution, the document recommends focusing on approaches that separate identity from location while maintaining incremental deployability. The analysis identifies common themes and trade-offs that inform future routing architecture work.

today: RFC 6115 represents the culmination of the RRG's work and remains an important reference for routing architecture research. While the group's recommendations have not led to a single standardized solution, the analysis continues to inform discussions about Internet scaling and has influenced later work on routing, such as LISP development and other locator/identifier separation approaches.

sections.title: The Routing Scaling Crisis
sections.content:
For decades, the Internet routing system has worked by combining two concepts: each device has an address that identifies both who it is and where it is on the network topology. This worked well when the Internet was small, but as billions of devices connect, the system faces three critical problems. First, the global routing table—the master list of all networks and how to reach them—has grown exponentially and now contains hundreds of thousands of entries, straining router memory and processing. Second, organizations using multiple Internet service providers (multihoming) must advertise multiple routes for the same networks, worsening the routing table bloat. Third, network operators lack effective tools to control where traffic flows across multiple connections (inter-domain traffic engineering).

The Internet Research Task Force's Routing Research Group (RRG) was chartered to research and recommend a new architecture. From March 2007 to March 2010, the group met regularly and discussed many proposals. This document captures the results of that effort, presenting proposals from the research community and the chairs' architectural recommendations.
sections.plainLanguage: As the internet grows bigger, everyone's router has to remember too many addresses. The RRG researched different ways to fix this problem.

sections.title: Identity, Location, and Core Concepts
sections.content:
To evaluate proposals, the RRG first established shared terminology. A locator is a topology-dependent name that describes where something is on the network—like an IP routing prefix. An identifier is topology-independent and describes what something is—like a domain name. An address in today's Internet combines both roles: an IPv4 or IPv6 address tells you both the identity and the location of a device.

The group reached broad consensus on several key insights. First, separating identity from location is desirable and technically feasible, but there is disagreement on how to do it best. Second, any solution must support multihoming efficiently and cost-effectively, not just for large enterprises but for all users. Third, solutions must be deployable incrementally; you cannot require every router on the Internet to change at the same time. Finally, the group agreed that solutions should preserve security and avoid creating new routing vulnerabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: Your address on the internet is like a name that also tells where you live. The group thought it would be better to separate these, but they disagreed on the best way.

sections.title: The Main Architectural Approaches
sections.content:
The proposals fall into several categories. Locator/identifier separation approaches like LISP, RANGI, and ILNP separate the address space into stable identifiers (for end hosts) and topology-dependent locators (for routing). LISP uses encapsulation to tunnel traffic through the existing Internet, requiring changes only at the edges. RANGI places an identifier layer between the network and transport layers. ILNP modifies the semantics of IP addresses to split them into identifier and locator components.

Hierarchical aggregation schemes like hIPv4 propose organizing addresses in a hierarchy that allows better route aggregation. Mapping systems like CRM and LMS introduce external databases that map identifiers to locators, decoupling the routing table from the addressing scheme. Two-phased mapping uses a mapping system only for traffic that needs it, avoiding changes to most routers. Other approaches like Evolution propose growing the system gracefully, and Name-Based Sockets suggest APIs that work with names rather than addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Some ideas separate your identity from your location. Others organize addresses better. Some use address lookup systems like a phone book. All try to solve the problem in different ways.

sections.title: Technical Trade-offs and Challenges
sections.content:
Each proposal offers distinct advantages and costs. LISP promises day-one benefits for early adopters and production implementations are underway, but it requires mapping infrastructure and has initial packet delays. RANGI achieves strong security and good mobility support but requires host and router changes. ILNP separates identity from location cleanly at the protocol level but faces challenges with session state. hIPv4 leverages IPv4 infrastructure but offers limited scalability. Mapping-based systems avoid router changes but shift complexity to the mapping layer and create distributed query systems that introduce latency.

Across all proposals, common trade-offs emerge. Approaches that minimize router changes push complexity to end hosts or edge routers. Approaches that promise the most scalability often require the most deployment effort. Mapping systems offer flexibility but create new infrastructure and potential bottlenecks. Identity/location separation solves the scalability problem but introduces new complexities in mobility, multihoming, and addressing schemes.
sections.plainLanguage: Every idea is good at some things but hard in other ways. One might be fast but need many changes. Another might work with old routers but not scale as well.

sections.title: The Path Forward
sections.content:
The group did not reach consensus on a single solution. Instead, the RRG chairs recommend focusing on approaches that clearly separate identity from location because this design principle directly addresses the root cause of the scaling problem. The chairs suggest that such an approach should have clear answers to several architectural questions: how to handle multihoming at scale, how to ensure efficient and timely delivery of mapping information, how to support both mobility and multihoming, how to handle the transition from the current architecture, and how to keep end systems and core routers largely unchanged during deployment.

The document notes that experience with deployment will be essential. No proposal can be definitively proven superior without real-world testing. The IETF should pursue the most promising approaches through incremental, monitored deployment and learn from operational experience. The research community should continue exploring alternatives, as the optimal solution may not yet be fully developed.
sections.plainLanguage: The group suggests picking ideas that separate identity from location, but they say the real answer will come from trying them out on the real internet and learning what works.
